items.title: Staying on the topic of interest rates, this from Bloomberg on market expectations for central bank policies: "Traders see borrowing costs rising faster in Japan, Canada, the euro zone and the UK than in the US over the next year. items.title: While on economic activity in Asia, China’s July industrial production growth slowed to 4.5%, missing the consensus forecast. Combined with lower-than-expected retail sales, today’s IP numbers confirm the narrative of a dual-track Chinese economy that spans both supply and demand factors: One consists of booming sectors fueled by tech and strong exports. The other is dominated by struggling sectors comprising more traditional production and weak domestic consumption. #economy #markets #China #growth #Asia

items.title: Japan’s Q2 GDP Growth Misses Expectations At an annualized rate of 1.1%, Japan's second-quarter GDP growth fell short of both the prior quarter’s 2.1% and the 2.0% consensus forecast. The policy implications of this miss are more consequential given the domestic measures required to support the yen, particularly as the impact of the joint currency intervention continues to erode (please see weekly note). Meanwhile, market pressure remains evident, with 10-year Japanese government bond yields rising to 2.92%, the highest level since 1996. (Reuters headline below.) #economy #Japan #growth #yen #currency

items.title: The always-thoughtful Olivier Blanchard examines the multiple equilibria aspects of France’s fiscal situation. (This analytical framework is also applicable to some other economies.) #economy #markets @ojblanchard1 #debt
items.content:
The always-thoughtful Olivier Blanchard examines the multiple equilibria aspects of France’s fiscal situation.
(This analytical framework is also applicable to some other economies.)
 #economy   #markets   @ojblanchard1   #debt Olivier Blanchard (@ojblanchard1)Many comments on the tweet about the risk of a public debt crisis in France point to the role of the central bank, the ECB in this case, in avoiding multiple equilibria. And, indeed, the ECB has a major role to play.

On paper, it is easy.

There are three zones, determined by fundamentals. At one end, the safe zone: debt is clearly sustainable. At the other end, the default zone: debt is clearly unsustainable. In the middle, the danger zone, where there are multiple equilibria, a good and a bad one., with the bad one leading to a crisis.

If in the safe zone, no need for the central bank to do anything. If in the default zone, need to adjust fiscal policy; not the job of the central bank. If in the danger zone, maintain the good equilibrium, by standing ready to buy if the private investors sell.

This is indeed the mandate of the ECB. If debt is clearly not sustainable, do not intervene unless there is an adjustment program which reestablishes sustainability. If in the danger zone, intervene to keep the interest low and debt sustainable.

In reality, things are not so simple.

When investors require a higher risk premium, how to tell whether we are in the danger zone and the ECB should intervene, or we are already in the default zone, in which case, short an adjustment program, it should not?

The reality: The ECB does not know for sure. And it is likely to be conservative, insist on an adjustment program, with or without a haircut or reprofiling, before intervening. Counting on the ECB to intervene to eliminate multiple equilibria, or even more so, to intervene when debt is clearly unsustainable is unwise.—  https://x.com/ojblanchard1/status/2088595673683722338 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Aug 15, 2026

items.title: Key Takeaways from this morning’s UMich US Consumer Sentiment Survey: The preliminary August consumer sentiment index fell to 51.0 (down from 55.2 in July), well below the consensus forecast of 55.0. Cost-of-living worries contributed to the decline, with survey director Joanne Hsu citing "notably large reductions… among older consumers, lower-income consumers, and those without a college degree." Consistent with the recent rebound in gasoline prices, year-ahead inflation expectations edged higher to 4.3%, while the 5–10 year measure printed at 3.3%. On a positive note, consumer concerns regarding employment remained relatively low. #economy #markets #inflation #employment #affordability
items.content:
Key Takeaways from this morning’s UMich US Consumer Sentiment Survey:
The preliminary August consumer sentiment index fell to 51.0 (down from 55.2 in July), well below the consensus forecast of 55.0.
Cost-of-living worries contributed to the decline, with survey director Joanne Hsu citing "notably large reductions… among older consumers, lower-income consumers, and those without a college degree."
Consistent with the recent rebound in gasoline prices, year-ahead inflation expectations edged higher to 4.3%, while the 5–10 year measure printed at 3.3%.
On a positive note, consumer concerns regarding employment remained relatively low.
 #economy   #markets   #inflation   #employment   #affordability 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Aug 14, 2026
